hints: Look at the order around the circle after cytokinesis. The very large stage 3 comes first, then stage 1, then the short stage 2 just before cytokinesis again.
Remember when two-chromatid chromosomes first appear and when they disappear. Think DNA replication in S phase to sister separation in anaphase of mitosis.
walkthrough:
**Label the stages in order**

Start just after cytokinesis and follow the arrow round. The cell grows first, then copies DNA, then divides.

In this diagram stage 3 is the long G1 growth phase, stage 1 is S phase plus G2, and stage 2 is the short mitosis phase just before cytokinesis.

**Decide when sister chromatids exist**

A chromosome is normally one chromatid with one DNA molecule. It only becomes two sister chromatids joined at the centromere after DNA replication.

$$S \ phase: DNA \ replicates \rightarrow two-chromatid \ chromosomes \ form$$
They stay like this through G2, prophase and metaphase, until the centromeres divide and sisters separate in anaphase.

**Match to stages 1, 2 and 3**

Stage 1 includes late S and all of G2, so for much of stage 1 sister chromatids are present. Stage 2 is mitosis, so prophase and metaphase also have sister chromatids joined by a centromere.

Stage 3 is G1 before replication, so chromosomes are single chromatid. Therefore only 1 and 2 include the two-chromatid period.

options.A: Correct. Stage 1 (S + G2) contains chromosomes after replication, and stage 2 (mitosis) contains them up to anaphase.
options.B: Stage 3 is G1 before DNA replication, so chromosomes there are single chromatids, not sister pairs.
options.C: Stage 2 is correct for mitosis, but stage 3 is too early in the cycle to have completed replication.
options.D: Stage 2 alone is incomplete because stage 1 also includes G2 when replicated sister chromatids are already present.
